edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1   1 (page number at right on every page)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>" on all six pages.

edits.quote: For each shape, circle the player who can always win: first or second.
edits.fix: "Can always win" is abstract for K-1, and children will just circle whoever won one game. Ask them to play each shape several times, taking turns going first, then circle who can win every time: first or second. Answers: hexagon second, strip first, trapezoid first. Put the mirror-strategy follow-up in the adult notes.

k-1.summary: A strong K-1 band. It has six physical problems on actual-size boards: impossible shapes, fewest green triangles (2, 3, 4, then predict 5), all coverings of two shapes (2 and 3 ways), flip puzzles (2 and 4 moves) and a take-away game whose answers are correct. All diagrams check out. The only edits are the footer and the phrasing of the game question.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1   1 (page number at right on every page)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>" on all nine pages.

edits.quote: Page 2 holds only boards E and F with no problem label and is about 55% blank; page 3 holds only triangles A and B of Problem 2 and its lower half is blank.
edits.fix: Reflow the pages. Start Problem 2 (triangles A and B) on page 2 under boards E and F, and put triangles C and D on the next page. This removes one page and keeps E and F from appearing as an unlabeled orphan page.

edits.quote: Could triangle C in Problem 2 be covered with blue blocks and fewer green triangles than you used? Explain.
edits.fix: The answer depends on the child's earlier result: a child who used 6 answers "yes" and the proof disappears. Ask: "What is the fewest green triangles that triangle C needs? Explain why no covering can use fewer."

edits.quote: so that it cannot be covered with blue blocks and fewer than 4 green triangles.
edits.fix: Remove the double negative: "...so that any covering of it with blue blocks and green triangles needs at least 4 green triangles."

grades-2-3.summary: This band covers kernel 1 completely and correctly. It moves from possible and impossible boards to hexagons with holes (A and D can be covered, B and C cannot), fewest gaps in triangles of side 2 to 5, a general rule for sides 10 and 100, purple versus blue (4/5/4/5 versus 2/3/4/5), and an invention problem. Every board is at actual size and checks out. The edits are small: reflow the page breaks and reword two prompts.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1   1 (page number at right on every page)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>" on all nine pages.

edits.quote: The blank small drawings of boards are for recording.
edits.fix: Delete this sentence. Each problem already says to draw in the copies.

edits.quote: Could the first pair in Problem 3 be done in fewer moves than you used? Could a round trip in Problem 4 take exactly 5 moves, or exactly 7 moves? Explain.
edits.fix: The first question depends on the child's own count, and the second repeats Problem 4. Rewrite as: "What is the fewest moves for the first pair in Problem 3? Prove that no shorter way exists. Prove that no round trip takes an odd number of moves." Answers: 8 moves (each chain goes from LLRR to RRLL); 5 and 7 are impossible.

edits.quote: Four small copies under the 1-3-3 hexagon board, plus "If you run out of copies, you can draw more on the back."
edits.fix: This board has 20 coverings, but there are only 4 copies, and the blank back has no grid. Add a page of about 20 compact gridded copies, or shrink the copies so that 16 to 20 fit.

edits.quote: Sixteen small copies of the big hexagon, plus "If you run out of copies, you can draw more on the back."
edits.fix: The big hexagon has 20 coverings. Add a fifth row of four copies in the empty bottom third of the page and delete the "back of the page" sentence.

grades-4-5.summary: This band is an excellent development of kernel 2, and every claim checks out. The (2,1,2) board has 6 coverings and a 6-edge flip graph. The flip pairs in Problem 3 take 8 and 4 moves. Round trips are possible in 4 and 6 moves but not 5 or 7. The chain definitions are consistent (example RLLR), two of the four chain pairs in Problem 6 are possible, and Problems 9 and 10 each have 20 coverings. The edits are minor: footer, one meta sentence, a prompt keyed to the child's own count, and not enough recording copies for the two counting problems.

overall.strongest: Grades 4–5 develop flips and ribbons through a well-chosen sequence, from listing coverings and the flip graph to fewest-move routes, the parity of round trips, chain constraints and full enumeration, and every diagram and answer is correct.
overall.weakest: The remaining problems are small and practical: non-standard footers, a few prompts that depend on the child's own earlier count (2–3 P4, 4–5 P8), awkward page breaks in grades 2–3, and too few recording copies for the 20-covering counts in grades 4–5.
